script.analysis: Full 25329 canonical characters read. A cold-open teaser of the last clips (sovereign-citizen loan claim), then a list of about 20 third-party clips, each followed by host commentary that quantifies the mistake and closes with a one-line moral. Arc: from comedy (Apple dollars) through overspending, taxes, credit, gambling and windfalls to legal consequences, ending on the "most confidently wrong" clip. Reproduced arithmetic: 4x overspend, about $40K on a $25-26K 17% car loan, $1,716 of annual interest, 46.2% interest share, $21,600 a year. Corrections: $143 on $6K implies about 28.6% APR, above the Fed G.19 average of 21-22%, not "standard". Verified: BoE confirms banks create most money by lending, supporting the host's nuanced rebuttal; IRS FMV rule for prizes. Clip facts are self-reported and unverified; speakers are not reliably separated in stored text.

topic.analysis: Consumer financial literacy failures: payments, overspending, credit-card and auto-loan interest, prize taxation, gambling, windfall management, speculative investing, leveraged housing, debt collection and pseudo-legal debt avoidance.
topic.audience_problem: Viewers seeking entertaining cautionary tales and quick quantified lessons on common money mistakes.
topic.time_sensitivity: Medium: card APR levels, PFIN year and high-yield rates are date-bound; mistakes are evergreen.
topic.narrative_angle: Countdown of escalating mistakes, each converted into one arithmetic lesson, ending on the most confidently wrong claim.
topic.novelty_and_corpus_angle: Test an original commentary format using licensed or user-submitted (consented) cases, where each mistake is quantified on screen (interest paid, APR implied, tax owed) against an official benchmark (Fed G.19 card APR, IRS prize-income rules), turning ridicule into a reproducible lesson.
topic.competition: Same-channel nearest-age peers in K01; not an independent niche or causal test
